<ANSWER>3</ANSWER>

The provided statements define a collection of ancestor-descendant relations that can be represented as directed edges in a graph (with the direction of each edge running from ancestor to descendant). All statements are consistent with a single linear chain containing every individual exactly once; each given relation corresponds to a forward (ancestor-to-descendant) step along this chain.

Angela appears at one end of the chain; the unique sequence of edges beginning at Angela reaches, among many other nodes,
\[
\text{Angela}\to\text{Randy}\to\dots\to\text{Catherine}\to\text{Wayne}\to\dots\to\text{Thomas}\to\text{Roy}\to\text{Jerry}.
\]
Consequently the transitive closure of the graph contains the pair (Angela, Jerry), which means Angela is an ancestor of Jerry.

Because the chain is linear and Angela is the topmost node, the two individuals have no common ancestor. Because Jerry is the bottommost node, the two individuals have no common descendant. The opposite relation (Angela is Jerry's descendant) would require a path in the reverse direction, which does not exist. Therefore only statement 3 holds.

Angela only directly appears as Randy's ancestor, and Jerry appears elsewhere like Roy's descendant, but without a direct link between Angela and Jerry through the chains, it seemed like they aren't related in a way that matches the options one to four. After piecing together the tree, nothing indicated acommon ancestor, descendant, or direct ancestry between Angela and Jerry, so the conclusion was that none of the statements 1 to 4 fit, making option 5 correct.So, the answer is 5.
